passage.title: Reading the Whitewater V
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Cold mist rose from the Chattahoochee River as Jalen and his older cousin Devon pushed their yellow kayaks off the gravel bank. Ahead of them, pine bluffs framed the wide brown channel. Jalen gripped his paddle tightly and stared downstream. A low roar grew louder every second. Half a mile ahead lay the remains of a nineteenth-century stone weir, an angled rock dam once built to guide water toward old brick textile mills.

While Jalen wanted to paddle straight down the middle of the river to save time, Devon tapped the deck of his boat and shook his head. He pointed to a line of white foam stretching across the center of the ledge. Submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam, were still avoided by local paddlers during high water. If a kayak rode straight over those flat rocks, the spinning wave at the base could trap the boat.

Devon paddled into a calm pocket of water behind a wide rock. There they could scout the drop together. Inside this quiet eddy, the water actually curled backward against the main flow, holding their boats steady like a natural parking spot. Standing up in his foot pegs, Devon showed Jalen two shapes on the water. Where hidden rocks blocked the river, a white V pointed upstream as a warning. Near the left bank, a dark, smooth tongue of water formed a clear V pointing downstream.

Jalen took a deep breath and followed Devon out of the calm eddy. He angled his bow toward that downstream V. Instead of fighting the river's pull with frantic strokes, he used short, crisp sweeps on his right side. Those smooth strokes lined his kayak up with the chute. The river caught his boat and slid him cleanly through the gap between the mossy stones. Spray splashed across his life vest as the bow bounced once and glided into the deep pool below.

Jalen turned his kayak into the next eddy and grinned as Devon pulled up beside him. Five minutes ago, the roaring ledge had looked like a wall of random foam. Now Jalen saw that the river wrote clear signs on its surface for anyone patient enough to pause and read them.

tier2Words.definition: completely covered by water; sitting below the surface
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root mergere ('to dip or plunge') + prefix sub- ('under')
tier2Words.contextClue: The granite blocks from the broken mill weir sat hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam.

tier2Words.definition: moving about roughly with swirling foam and splashes
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English cyrin, referring to stirring or tossing liquid strongly
tier2Words.contextClue: White foam and spinning waves tossed roughly over the hidden rocks of the ledge.

tier2Words.definition: a calm circular current of water behind an obstacle that flows backward against the main stream
tier2Words.rootHint: From Old English ed- ('back, again'), describing water turning back
tier2Words.contextClue: Behind the wide boulder, the water curled backward against the main flow and held their boats steady like a parking spot.

tier2Words.definition: wild, hurried, and out of control from fear or worry
tier2Words.contextClue: Instead of fighting the river with wild, rushed strokes, Jalen used short, crisp sweeps to line up his boat.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam, were still avoided by local paddlers during high water."

Which active-voice rewrite preserves the exact meaning of this sentence?

options.text: Churning surface foam avoided the local paddlers and hid the broken mill weir during high water.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action around! Surface foam is just bubbly water on the river—local paddlers are the people who avoided the hidden granite blocks.

options.text: Submerged granite blocks chased local paddlers across the broken mill weir during high water.
options.childFeedback: Heavy granite blocks sitting on the river bottom cannot chase paddlers! Instead, local paddlers avoided the submerged blocks.

options.text: Local paddlers still avoided the submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, which sat hidden beneath the foam.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by local paddlers' right after 'were still avoided' shows that local paddlers are the ones who avoided the submerged granite blocks hidden beneath the foam.

options.text: Workers from the old brick textile mills rebuilt the granite blocks to block kayaks.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says the stone weir was built back in the nineteenth century for old brick textile mills; no mill workers are rebuilding it today.

questions.provingSentenceText: Submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam, were still avoided by local paddlers during high water.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by local paddlers' right after 'were still avoided' shows that local paddlers are the ones who avoided the submerged granite blocks hidden beneath the foam.
questions.parentExplanation: In the passive clause 'Submerged granite blocks... were still avoided by local paddlers', the actor is 'local paddlers' and the receiver is 'Submerged granite blocks'. Option B restores active voice accurately.
questions.retryHint: Look at the 'by' phrase right after 'were still avoided' in Paragraph 2 to see who did the avoiding.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam, were still avoided by local paddlers during high water."

What does the word submerged mean as it is used in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Covered by water below the surface
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, 'submerged' means covered by water below the surface, as shown by the clue 'hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam.'

options.text: Stacked high on the dry gravel bank
options.childFeedback: Sitting on the dry gravel bank is the opposite of being 'hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam' in the middle of the river.

options.text: Carved into smooth wooden paddles
options.childFeedback: Granite is hard gray rock from the broken dam, not wood carved into kayak paddles.

options.text: Painted bright yellow like a kayak
options.childFeedback: The cousins' kayaks were yellow in Paragraph 1, whereas the submerged granite blocks were hidden underwater beneath white foam.

questions.provingSentenceText: Submerged granite blocks from the broken mill weir, hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam, were still avoided by local paddlers during high water.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, 'submerged' means covered by water below the surface, as shown by the clue 'hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam.'
questions.parentExplanation: The phrase 'hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam' provides a direct context clue that 'submerged' means underwater.
questions.retryHint: Look at the clue right after ' broken mill weir' in Paragraph 2: 'hidden just inches beneath the churning surface foam.'

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, how do Jalen's and Devon's boats stay still behind the wide rock while they scout the drop?

options.text: The river stops flowing completely whenever the morning mist rises from the channel.
options.childFeedback: The main river keeps roaring downstream—only the small pocket of water behind the wide rock curls backward to hold the boats still.

options.text: They tie their yellow kayaks to an iron ring bolted into the old brick textile mill.
options.childFeedback: The cousins never tie their boats to an iron ring on the old mill; they float in the calm eddy behind a wide rock while Devon stands up in his foot pegs.

options.text: They drag their boats onto the dry pine bluffs high above the Chattahoochee River.
options.childFeedback: They stay on the water inside the quiet eddy rather than dragging their kayaks up onto the high pine bluffs.

options.text: The water inside the eddy curls backward against the main flow, holding their kayaks in place.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that inside the quiet eddy behind the wide rock, the water curls backward against the main river flow, holding their kayaks steady like a natural parking spot.

questions.provingSentenceText: Inside this quiet eddy, the water actually curled backward against the main flow, holding their boats steady like a natural parking spot.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that inside the quiet eddy behind the wide rock, the water curls backward against the main river flow, holding their kayaks steady like a natural parking spot.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that inside the eddy behind the rock, the water curls backward against the main flow, holding their kayaks steady so they can scout the drop.
questions.retryHint: Read the third sentence of Paragraph 3 to see how the water moves inside the quiet eddy.

questions.prompt: How do Jalen's approach and Devon's approach to the river differ in Paragraph 2?

options.text: Jalen wants to turn around and paddle back to the gravel bank, while Devon wants to jump over the dam.
options.childFeedback: Neither boy wants to turn back to the gravel bank; Jalen wants to paddle straight down the middle, while Devon guides him to scout a safe chute.

options.text: Jalen wants to rush straight down the center, while Devon insists on stopping to check for hidden hazards first.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 contrasts Jalen's impulse to paddle straight down the middle to save time with Devon's careful choice to stop and point out the hidden granite blocks under the foam.

options.text: Both boys refuse to wear life vests until they reach the deep pool below the stone weir.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 mentions spray splashing across Jalen's life vest, proving he is already wearing his life vest on the river.

options.text: Devon wants to paddle through the white upstream V, while Jalen chooses the left bank on his own.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, Devon explains that an upstream-pointing white V is a warning for hidden rocks, while the smooth downstream V near the left bank is the safe path.

questions.provingSentenceText: While Jalen wanted to paddle straight down the middle of the river to save time, Devon tapped the deck of his boat and shook his head.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 contrasts Jalen's impulse to paddle straight down the middle to save time with Devon's careful choice to stop and point out the hidden granite blocks under the foam.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 2 (ELAGSE5RL3), Jalen initially wants to take the fast shortcut straight down the middle, whereas Devon cautiously warns him about the submerged granite blocks and leads him into an eddy to scout.
questions.retryHint: Read the first two sentences of Paragraph 2 to compare what Jalen wants to do with how Devon responds.

questions.prompt: Part A: How does Jalen change from the beginning of the passage to the end?

options.text: He learns that paddling as hard and fast as possible is the only way to cross a stone weir.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says the exact opposite: instead of fighting the river with frantic strokes, Jalen uses short, smooth sweeps to line up with the chute.

options.text: He decides that kayaking on moving rivers is too dangerous and plans to stick to flat lakes.
options.childFeedback: Jalen grins in Paragraph 5 after gliding cleanly into the deep pool below—he feels confident about reading the river, not afraid of kayaking.

options.text: He shifts from seeing the rapids as confusing foam to understanding how to read surface clues for a safe path.
options.childFeedback: At first the roaring ledge looks like a wall of random foam to Jalen, but after Devon shows him the upstream and downstream V shapes, Jalen understands how to pause and read the river's surface signs.

options.text: He discovers how nineteenth-century mill workers cut granite blocks from the river bluffs.
options.childFeedback: The nineteenth-century stone weir is just the obstacle in the river; Jalen learns how to read whitewater currents, not how historical workers cut stone.

questions.provingSentenceText: Now Jalen saw that the river wrote clear signs on its surface for anyone patient enough to pause and read them.
questions.childTip: At first the roaring ledge looks like a wall of random foam to Jalen, but after Devon shows him the upstream and downstream V shapes, Jalen understands how to pause and read the river's surface signs.
questions.parentExplanation: At first Jalen wants to charge down the middle and sees the ledge as a wall of random foam, but after Devon teaches him to spot eddies and the downstream V, Jalen learns to read the river's surface clues.
